Article Title: India and the tail: The old habit needs to die now
Article Text:
Head coach Gautam Gambhir with captain Shubman Gill (Photo: BCCI | X)

Wellington:

India have struggled to wrap up opposition innings over the years, and the problem has persisted since Shubman Gill took over as captain ahead of the England tour last year. In the 12 Tests played under his leadership, opposition lower-order batters have repeatedly frustrated India, scoring crucial runs from No. 8 onwards.England's lower order added 369 runs in eight innings, the West Indies scored 201 in four, while South Africa accumulated 213 in just three.The most frustrating runs came during the recent away series against Sri Lanka, where India conceded 145 runs in four innings and saw the opposition tail survive for 95.2 overs. This played a major role in India missing out on crucial World Test Championship (WTC) points, as the Colombo Test ended in a draw.In the upcoming Test series against New Zealand, India need to be wary of the lower-order threat, as the hosts have bowlers who are more than handy with the bat. In lively conditions, 30-40 extra runs can significantly affect the contest. This was evident in the fifth ODI, when Mohammed Siraj and Arshdeep Singh's useful contributions at Nos. 10 and 11 proved decisive.Bowling coach Morne Morkel acknowledged that this is a "very important" area, as New Zealand have bowlers capable of putting together small, but very crucial, partnerships."Very important. At the end of the day, to win a Test match, you need to bowl the team out. Like I said, we always respect and do a lot of work with lower-order batters. Gone are the days when you can just start the heavy roller and get those right, because those crucial sort of partnerships we do see happen more often," Morkel told reporters in Wellington."If you look at the New Zealand lower order, they're all guys who are capable of getting small-level partnerships. I think for us it's going to be crucial that we understand that, acknowledge that, and still do the things that help us get the wickets, sort of bowling the top order out," Morkel said.During the Sri Lanka series, India were tactically exposed because there were passages of play when they never looked to dismiss the set batters. Open fields became common, allowing the tailenders to buy time and grow in confidence as the innings and partnerships progressed. Morkel felt that not being "a little bit greedy" would be important, and said they had plans to prevent the tail from wagging."I think at times we can get a little bit greedy, get carried away, and then before you know it, there's a 20- or 30-run partnership, or guys find a little bit of comfort at the crease. So how we can attack that better, can we be more aggressive maybe with a short ball, a field setting, but still, a good ball is a good ball on any wicket, and can we test the defence of a tailender more consistently from both ends," Morkel explained.The former South African fast bowler, who has experience playing in these conditions and was particularly effective at cleaning up the lower order, called for a more proactive approach from both ends."I think at times we were maybe a little bit, a little bit sort of missing our mark from both ends in terms of knocking the tail over, in terms of bowling combinations at the time, expecting it will happen and not actually committing to it," Morkel said.Gill has repeatedly spoken about how quickly momentum can shift because of frustrating lower-order contributions. He has regularly called for his bowlers to contribute in this regard and will now need to be on top of his tactical game to ensure opposition lower-order batters do not run away with the momentum.
Article Summary: India have struggled to wrap up opposition innings over the years. The problem has persisted since Shubman Gill took over as captain ahead of the England tour last year. England's lower order added 369 runs in eight innings, the West Indies scored 201 in four, while South Africa accumulated 213 in just three.

Article Title: Magnus Carlsen didn't show up for fast classical chess: Who is at fault?
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: During the players' group photoshoot before the Total Chess Pilot event in Budapest, Hungary, five-time world champion and current World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen was one of the last to arrive, climbing a couple of stairs to sneak into the group photo from the back and finding his place beside Kazakh Grandmaster Bibisara Assaubayeva.Soon, cutouts and clips of the two standing together started doing the rounds, captioned along the lines of "no weak characters" and "imagine the number of World Championships they share between them" — 23 in total, Carlsen alone accounting for 20.Little did anyone know that both would end up sitting across the board in a match to decide 17th-21st place in this pilot event, and that one of them choosing not to show up for the day's final game would put them at the centre of a heated debate Carlsen had already sealed the match before a single Fast Classical move was played. He beat Assaubayeva 3-0 in Blitz with one draw, and 2-0 in Rapid, putting the score at 11.5-0.5. The match was decided, regardless of what happened next.Before the Fast Classical round began, Carlsen walked out of the playing hall. Asked why by Norwegian media outlet TV2, he said, "There will be no classical game as I understood, the match is over.The only consequence of not showing up is that you will lose a totally useless game. I think that if you play a World Championship and it counts for points and such, I can understand. But this is not a show tournament. If the match is done, it's done. In the end, if you play games after, it shall not be rated because it's always been like that. And if they want to do things differently here... yeah. This is my decision on this topic."After the mandatory 15-minute default period, Assaubayeva walked out too, awarded the win on forfeit. Day 1 of the semifinal closed 11.5-8.5 in Carlsen's favour. The game, which was supposed to count towards FIDE ratings, went unplayed and therefore had no impact on either player's classical rating.Chief arbiter Anastasia Sorokina, speaking to ChessBase India at the venue, confirmed that any further penalties for the forfeit would be at the organisers' discretion."The result is minus-plus because Magnus didn't appear for the game. From our perspective as arbiters, there are no extra penalties for this, except the game is minus-plus, of course," she said."There is a point about the possible fees that organisers could apply, but it's not directly connected to the game. So it depends on the situation, organisers will decide."Under FIDE's regulations, forfeited games don't count toward classical ratings, which is precisely what made the decision rational for Carlsen.He'd had a torn group stage in the Fast Classical format, failing to win any of his 10 games, drawing nine and losing one to Armenia's Haik Martirosyan, a run that cost him 21.8 Elo points and pushed his live rating down to 2801.2, uncomfortably close to Hikaru Nakamura and Fabiano Caruana overtaking him as World No. 1.A draw against Assaubayeva would have cost him 3.5 more rating points, a defeat 8.5. By forfeiting, he avoided both, since an unplayed game carries no rating consequence at all. Total Chess founder and CEO Kjell Madland also shared his view on the situation."He (Carlsen) was there and discussed it with the arbiter team. The system is to win the day, and he had already won enough points to win the day. So then he didn't want to play the last game, and he didn't need to do it," he told ChessBase India.On whether Assaubayeva was informed beforehand, he replied, "No, because he could play if he wanted to play. We of course didn't discuss this with Bibisara before, that was not necessary."Pressed on whether the rules might change after this forfeit, Madland added, "The rules are the same for everyone. We can't do any differences between the players. It's the same for everyone. So if that happens tomorrow with someone else, it happened."Calling Budapest "an important learning exercise" ahead of the tour's inaugural edition in March 2027, the organisers stressed they weren't approaching the feedback "with a predetermined view that the rules need to change".Whatever the rules allowed, there was a simpler courtesy Carlsen could have extended and chose not to. By his own account, and the organisers’, he had already decided against playing and discussed the matter with the arbiter team before the round began. The decision, therefore, had been made well before Assaubayeva took her seat at the board.However, with no prior communication, Assaubayeva was left waiting through the full 15-minute default period for an opponent who had no intention of showing up.The rulebook may have little to say about such omissions, governing forfeits rather than the courtesy of forewarning, but it is difficult to separate the question of sportsmanship from the technicalities of the regulations.A simple two-line message through the arbiters would have cost Carlsen nothing and spared Assaubayeva an entirely unnecessary wait.That it never came makes this less a question of what the rules required and more one of the basic consideration an opponent deserves.American Grandmaster Hans Niemann took to social media to voice his concerns. "It was already known that we have to play all the games, we talked about it in the technical meeting," he wrote on X."It's incredibly disappointing to see continued favouritism towards one player. Let's not forget the jeans, and 'Co World Champion' saga. All rules must be applied equally, regardless of the player."Alireza Firouzja noted the same technical meeting had addressed it directly, though Norwegian outlet TV2 reported Carlsen wasn't present for that meeting.Wesley So, on the other hand, saw little wrong with the logic."I think Magnus' decision was understandable. He already won the match, and if he lost to Bibi, he loses 9 points and the No. 1 spot. I don't see yet why Magnus was wrong," he wrote on X.Every answer in this saga is technically correct, and that's precisely the problem. The rules allowed it, the arbiters applied them without penalty, and Carlsen broke no regulation in walking out.But a pilot event exists to surface exactly this kind of gap, between what the rulebook permits and what the field considers fair, before it hardens into precedent.India's Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa, who lost 19.3 rating points of his own in this pilot event, raised a broader gripe about dead-rubber games."It doesn't matter if you finish sixth in the group stage, you still have to play, which is kind of, honestly, sad," he said in an interview with Total Chess. "By that point the player has already started thinking about the next tournament, but he still has to play a game."With the inaugural Total Chess World Championship Tour arriving in March 2027, the organisation now has a concrete decision to make: whether a dead-rubber game, once a match is mathematically settled, should exist at all, or whether, if it does, every player is held to showing up regardless of stakes.Leaving that ambiguous is what turned one player's rational choice into a credibility question for the format itself.It also calls for a separate conversation about the structure of a tournament like this, with some players seemingly unhappy with the number of games scheduled each day across the different formats."I just felt envious that you can solve the sports part in Rapid and Blitz portion and then have a nice evening without chess, which is understandable because we have five days in a row with two rounds every day," Russian Grandmaster Ian Nepomniachtchi told ChessBase India. "Of course, there was a rest day, but it was overall a bit tiring."
Article Summary: Magnus Carlsen didn't show up for fast classical chess against Bibisara Assaubayeva. Carlsen had already sealed the match before a single Fast Classical move was played. The game, which was supposed to count towards FIDE ratings, went unplayed and had no impact on either player's classical rating.

Article Title: Arin Ahuja rides waves of golf, dreams of making it big on global stage
Article Text:
Arin Ahuja (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For 22-years-old Arin Ahuja, golf was never part of a carefully drawn career plan. It began with a simple family routine in 2011, when his father, who was associated with the US Golf Club in Mumbai started taking him and his brother along to the course. What started as a way to spend an afternoon soon developed into a passion, eventually setting him on the path towards professional golf.At just seven years old, Arin, who is from Noida, found himself fascinated by the game. Initially, it was all about hitting a few balls, playing around with the golf carts and challenging the caddies to put on contests. However, those casual visits gradually turned into something much bigger. Fifteen years later, the young golfer is beginning to make his mark, having topped the Professional Golf Tour of India (PGTI) Qualifying School and taken a significant step towards establishing himself on the professional circuit.The transition from amateur golf to the professional circuit, however, has brought an entirely different set of challenges. Having spent the last few years competing in amateur tournaments, Arin is now learning what it takes to consistently compete against some of the country's established professionals."Once you make that shift, you need to be more deliberate about everything. You need to know yourself well, understand your statistics and record everything you do on the course so that you can improve. Playing 12 or 13 events a year on the national circuit also gives you more exposure. You learn how to analyse different situations, react to them and then work on those aspects after the tournament," he said.Arin draws inspiration from two of golf's biggest names, Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy. While both have influenced his approach to the sport, it is Woods' competitive mentality that particularly resonates with him."He just had that attitude where he needed to do it. He never backed down, no matter what. He wanted to win and was aggressive about everything. He was intimidating for other players as well. That inspired me to be a bit like him on the golf course," Arin said.However, the youngster is equally conscious of developing his own identity. Rather than getting distracted by what others are doing, he prefers to remain focused on his game and maintain control over his emotions.Golf, after all, is a sport of fine margins, where a disappointing round can quickly test a player's patience. Arin believes one of the most important lessons he has learnt is to accept setbacks rather than fight them. With tournaments regularly lined up on the calendar, he knows there is always another opportunity to put things right."If you have a bad tournament, I feel you should let the emotions sink in for a day or two. I am fortunate to have a good team behind me in the form of my parents and coach. We sit down, discuss what went wrong and what went right, and then go back to the drawing board to correct the mistakes," he explained.His triumph at the PGTI Qualifying School has provided further encouragement. For a young golfer making his way into the professional ranks, topping the qualifying event is an important confidence booster and an indication that the work being put in is beginning to deliver results.Arin is also optimistic about the growing opportunities within Indian professional golf. He believes the increasing prize money and competitiveness on the PGTI circuit have made the sport a more attractive career option for aspiring professionals."The PGTI has helped not just me but all the professionals on tour. The prize money has gone up, the competition has become tighter and there are so many more avenues open to players now. When you put in 7-8 hours every day at the golf course, winning an event like this is good validation that your hard work is paying off," he said.He believes that golfers who consistently perform among the top 40 on the domestic circuit can build a sustainable professional career, provided they continue to put in the necessary work.Beyond the technical aspects, Arin has also been working on developing a stronger mental approach. Since beginning his association with coach Raul, he feels certain technical adjustments have helped him find greater consistency."You understand over a period of time that golf is not always going to be up. It has its ups and downs, so you learn to accept that and not fight it too much. You just ride the waves. If things are going down, you know they will eventually go up again," he said.He also credits Indian golfer Shubhankar Sharma for offering valuable advice during a difficult phase. Following a disappointing tournament, a conversation with Sharma reinforced the importance of self-belief."He told me that you have to ride the waves in this game and trust yourself. Self-belief is the most important thing in golf. It takes you wherever you want to go," Arin recalled.But behind the youngster's progress is a support system that has remained his biggest strength. His father, who served in the Army, and his brother, who is also in the armed forces, have instilled in him a sense of discipline and perseverance. His mother, too, has been a constant source of encouragement."There have been moments when I felt like leaving the game because I wasn't playing well. But my family pushed me to keep going. My father and brother have that mindset that you always have to keep at it. Things are not easy, but you still have to persevere. It is because of them that I am here today," he said.For now, the ambition is to strengthen every aspect of his game, lower his scoring average and gradually earn opportunities to compete internationally. The ultimate dream is to make it to the PGA Tour, but Arin knows that the journey will require patience and consistent performances.Having already taken an important step with his Q-School triumph, Arin is beginning to turn childhood curiosity into professional ambition. And if there is one lesson he has carried from his journey so far, it is that success in golf is as much about believing in yourself through the difficult days as it is about celebrating the good ones.
Article Summary: Arin Ahuja has topped the Professional Golf Tour of India (PGTI) Qualifying School. The 22-year-old has spent the last few years competing in amateur tournaments. Arin draws inspiration from two of golf's biggest names, Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy.

Article Title: IND vs NZ 1st Test: Beware the Basin bluff! Shubman Gill's four-pacer plan looks beyond the first morning
Article Text:
Shubman Gill (AFP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The first thing that catches the eye at the Basin Reserve is the grass. Lots of it. On the banks and the outfield and plenty of it on the pitch too. The curators have left close to 15mm of cover on the surface, significantly more than the usual 6-8mm one is used to seeing at the start of Tests at most venues. It might create the impression of a classic seamer’s paradise ahead of Thursday’s first Test.Yet India seem to be wary of falling into that trap.Captain Shubman Gill , while speaking to the media, made repeated references to wanting bowlers who can “hit the deck hard”. It suggests the visitors want to plan for what the pitch could become on days three, four and five rather than just what it might offer in the opening session.“We’ve seen that on days three, four and five, especially with the old ball, the wicket can go a little flat,” Gill said while discussing team combinations.It is a view backed by history. While the Basin Reserve can provide movement under cloud cover early in the match, the surface often settles down considerably as the game progresses, with batting becoming easier once the lacquer fades off the Kookaburra ball and the green grass on the pitch changes to a straw-coloured stubble.Could that explain why Gill is thinking also about durability rather than just swing and seam?“We need at least a couple of bowlers who can hit the deck hard and bowl in the high-130s or 140-plus range.Once the Kookaburra ball gets old, the seam wears down and it doesn’t move as much off the pitch. That’s when you need bowlers who can hit the deck hard and keep creating chances.”The captain’s views provide clues about what India’s pace attack could be come Thursday.It’s clear India will play four fast bowlers, the selection debate described as “a headache, but a good kind of headache.”Under Gill and Gambhir, India have also valued lower-order runs, and that is why we have seen players like Nitish Kumar Reddy and Washington Sundar play overseas with Ravindra Jadeja as all-round options, with batting being the stronger suit of all three cricketers.However, when discussing the lower-order balance, Gill on Tuesday highlighted Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj for their batting abilities. It probably suggests a change of tactic.“Ideally, we’re looking at seven proper batsmen. The No. 8 and No. 9 spots will depend on the combination because Akash can bat a bit, Anshul can bat a bit.”Join the dots and what do you get? Not a happy picture if you happen to be Mohammed Siraj While Siraj remains one of India’s most experienced seamers and a proven new-ball operator, who helped India draw the series in England with a heroic performance at the Oval, Gill’s emphasis on lower-order runs, height, pace and second-innings effectiveness appears to favour bowlers such as Akash Deep, Kamboj and the rapid Gurnoor over a like-for-like seam option to support Jasprit Bumrah and Prasidh Krishna .Gill also acknowledged the unique wind factor of Wellington. “I think it’s actually tougher for the bowlers than the batters. If a bowler has to send down 15 or 20 overs and half of them are against the wind, it’s a very tough job.”That probably explains India’s desire for a varied attack capable of operating in different phases of the game. Gill was in the reserves six years ago when New Zealand exposed India at the Basin because man to man, they were better equipped for the conditions.As captain, he does not want a repeat. “They were better prepared and knew exactly how to exploit our weaknesses. That’s one reason we’re looking at four fast bowlers. You want bowlers who can exploit movement if it’s there and others who can bend their backs and hit hard lengths consistently if the ball isn’t doing much.”And that is why the final XI may be decided less by what the Basin Reserve looks like on Wednesday than by what Gill expects it to look like on Sunday.
Article Summary: India captain Shubman Gill wants bowlers who can ‘hit the deck hard’ Curators have left close to 15mm of cover on the Basin Reserve surface. Gill was in the reserves six years ago when New Zealand exposed India at the Basin.

Article Title: Sandpapergate fallout: Cricket Australia opens independent forum for players to share 2018 ball-tampering accounts
Article Text:
L-R: Usman Khawaja, David Warner; David Boon, and Todd Greenberg (AP Photos)

'Time for a circuit breaker': Boon explains CA's decision

Khawaja's claims reopen old wounds

'The game is hurting': Greenberg rules out fresh investigation

The bans that shook Australian cricket

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cricket Australia (CA) has announced plans to establish an independent forum for players and support staff involved in the controversial 2018 tour of South Africa, offering them an opportunity to share their versions of events in a confidential and respectful environment as the fallout from the ball-tampering scandal resurfaces.The decision comes in the wake of fresh allegations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, which have reignited the debate over how much the Australian dressing room knew about the infamous sandpaper incident in Cape Town. CA interim chairman David Boon said the forum would allow those involved to share their experiences and perspectives, nearly nine years after the scandal rocked Australian cricket.However, the governing body has made it clear that the initiative will not reopen its original investigation, nor will it lead to fresh sanctions. CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said the forum was intended to give everyone who wished to speak an independent, safe and private platform.Announcing the board's decision in Hobart on Wednesday, ahead of Australia's one-day international against England, Boon said the prolonged controversy had become a distraction for the sport."The CA Board agreed to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and their perspectives," Boon told reporters."For almost a decade, the fallout from these events has remained part of conversation around Australian cricket ... We believe it is time for a circuit breaker."In its official statement, CA said the forum would allow those who wished to come forward to share their recollections in a confidential environment. The board has opted against initiating a fresh investigation, believing that a forum would provide a better opportunity for everyone involved to speak constructively and with mutual respect.Boon stressed that the exercise was not about reopening old wounds but about allowing people to be heard."This forum is not about relitigating the past. It is about creating an opportunity for those who wish to be heard to tell their stories in a respectful environment, and for our sport to listen," he said.The former Australia batter also highlighted the importance of restoring relationships within the cricket fraternity."As a former player, I know that one of the most important things cricket gives us is the relationships we build and the mateship that endures long after playing careers end. My hope is that this process can help strengthen those connections and allow us to focus on what lies ahead," Boon added.The latest controversy follows claims in Khawaja's autobiography that contradicted the findings of CA's original investigation into the ball-tampering episode during the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town in March 2018.The initial probe concluded that only then captain Steve Smith , vice-captain David Warner and opening batter Cameron Bancroft were aware of the plan to use sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball.Bancroft was caught on television cameras attempting to scuff up the ball with a piece of sandpaper, triggering one of the biggest controversies in Australian cricket history.Khawaja's account, backed by Warner, suggested that the wider team was at least aware of the attempt to tamper with the ball. However, Test captain Pat Cummins and fellow fast bowler Mitchell Starc have maintained that they knew nothing about the plan.The revelations have once again brought the contrasting accounts of those involved into focus, prompting CA to provide an avenue for players and support staff who were not interviewed during the original investigation to share their recollections.Greenberg acknowledged that the latest developments had created an uncomfortable situation for Australian cricket, while also accepting that the governing body had a role in shaping the culture that existed at the time."Over the past week we have heard several different and conflicting accounts of what transpired in Cape Town in 2018. This has been an incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and all those involved," he said."What happened then and continues to play out now has a lot to do with the culture that existed at that time. A culture that CA played a part in creating."He also pointed to the Ethics Centre report commissioned after the scandal and the subsequent adoption of 36 of its 42 recommendations as part of the governing body's efforts to address cultural shortcomings.Greenberg said the new forum was an opportunity to give everyone a voice without turning it into another disciplinary exercise."This is a chance to give everyone a voice in an independent, safe and private setting," he said."This is not a re-investigation, it is not designed to reprosecute or sanction."Participation will be entirely voluntary, with no player or support staff member compelled to come forward. CA also does not intend to make the findings or accounts necessarily public."Let's be honest - the game is hurting at the moment," Greenberg said."It is not good for anyone. We need to find a path through and we need to heal."The 2018 ball-tampering scandal resulted in severe penalties for the three players identified by CA's original investigation. Smith and Warner were each handed 12-month bans from elite cricket for bringing the game into disrepute, while Bancroft received a nine-month suspension for his role in carrying the sandpaper onto the field.The episode also led to widespread scrutiny of Australia's team culture and prompted significant changes within the governing body.Eight years on, CA hopes the independent forum will help bring closure to a controversy that continues to divide opinions and affect those associated with the game."We hope everyone will respect this process and the players will be given the space they need to perform at their best during an important period for the game," Greenberg said.
Article Summary: Cricket Australia announces plans to establish an independent forum for players and support staff involved in the controversial 2018 tour of South Africa. The decision comes in the wake of fresh allegations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography. CA interim chairman David Boon said the forum would allow those involved to share their experiences and perspectives, nearly nine years after the scandal rocked Australian cricket.

Article Title: Digboi Golf: Despite leg injury, Rathi takes two-shot lead after first round
Article Text:
Saurav Rathi during the first round of Masters Golf tournament in Digboi, Assam, on Tuesday. (Pic credit: PGTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

DIGBOI: Away from Delhi-NCR’s hazardous air quality, Gurugram golfer Saurav Rathi topped the leaderboard with a seven-under 65 in the first round at Digboi Golf Links here on Tuesday.Playing with an injured leg, the 24-year-old made eight birdies and dropped his only shot of the day on the closing hole, a par-4 18th, to take a two-shot lead on an opening day when only 29 players from a field of 120 managed to break par. It was an impressive start to the 2026-27 PGTI season for Rathi at Assam’s iconic golf course.“It was a solid round and a good start to the new season. I was five-under after nine holes, made two more birdies on the 11th and 12th, followed by another birdie on the 14th. I made pars after that before dropping a disappointing bogey on the 18th from the middle of the fairway, just 40 yards out,” Rathi said after the round.Rathi was joined near the top by 21-year-old Anshul Kabthiyal and Players’ Championship 2026 winner Om Prakash Chouhan, who shared second place at five-under 67.Rathi, a regular on PGTI since 2019, recently secured his full playing rights for the new season after finishing 17th at PGTI Qualifying Tournament Final Stage in Ahmedabad.Despite nursing a leg injury sustained after slipping on wet stairs at the golf course on Monday, Rathi produced a commanding display, hitting 12 of 14 fairways and 15 greens in regulation.“I think the injury has actually helped me because I normally play a little fast. Since I’m not able to walk properly, I’ve had to slow myself down, and I think that’s helping my game,” he said, adding that he hoped to “strike the ball the same way I did today and make some putts”.Playing for the sixth time in India's longest-running golf tournament, Rathi also didn't shy away from expressing his appreciation of the weather here.“It’s a great course! I’m from Delhi and it's worth coming all the way here just because of the weather. The amenities here also very good, so I always like playing here.”Meanwhile, Kabthiyal’s opening 67 featured an eagle on the par-5 seventh, five birdies and two bogeys.The experienced Chouhan, an 11-time PGTI winner, former European Challenge Tour winner and the 2023 PGTI rankings champion, also carded a 67, making eight birdies against three bogeys.Four players shared fourth place at four-under 68, including Gurugram’s Kushal Singh, Pune’s Divyansh Dubey, Kapurthala’s Yuvraj Singh and Lucknow’s Sanjeev Kumar.Kushal made seven birdies and three bogeys, while Divyansh registered six birdies and two bogeys. Yuvraj recovered from a double-bogey on the par-5 15th and another bogey with seven birdies, while Sanjeev produced five birdies against a lone bogey.Despite measuring just 6,348 yards, the par-72 course presented a stern opening-round test, with only 29 players in the field returning sub-par scores.(The writer is in Digboi on an invitation from DP World PGTI)
Article Summary: Gurugram golfer Saurav Rathi cards seven-under 65 in first round of Masters Golf tournament in Digboi, Assam. The 24-year-old made eight birdies and dropped his only shot of the day on the closing hole, a par-4 18th. Only 29 players from a field of 120 managed to break par on an opening day.

Article Title: 'You cannot be a champion without working like one': Vivaan Kapoor on his Doha silver, Olympic dream
Article Text:
Vivaan Kapoor

NEW DELHI:

For shooter Vivaan Kapoor, winning a silver medal at the World Championships in Doha in the men's trap event was not just a reward for his hard work but also a reminder of how far he has come in a sport where one missed target can change everything. Having secured an Olympic quota for India, the young shooter is now focused on maintaining his form, making the most of the opportunities ahead and continuing his journey towards the biggest stage in sport."It was not easy because it was a very windy time when we went there. There were a lot of gusts of wind and even the second day was very gloomy. In shooting, especially in my event, it really matters whether it is cloudy or sunny because that depends on how you see the target," Kapoor said.However, he believes that dealing with such challenges is part of an athlete's preparation. "Wind is generally the toughest thing to keep control of. But in the end, it was the same for everybody. We train to be in such conditions and perform even when things are tough," he said.While technical ability remains central to shooting, Kapoor believes the mental side of the sport is what separates the best from the rest. With several shots to negotiate in quick succession, the ability to move on from a mistake can be the difference between a medal and a disappointing finish.For Kapoor, the key word is 'reset'."You cannot be a superhuman or a robot. It is normal to feel bad after missing a target. I tell myself, 'Okay, Vivaan, you are feeling bad about it. See what you did, try not to make that mistake the next time and move forward.' You don't have much time before your next shot, so you cannot get into a deep analysis. You have to understand the mistake and move on," he explained.He believes that champions are often distinguished by how quickly they can put a bad shot behind them rather than by whether they experience disappointment at all.Kapoor's recent progress has also been shaped by technical changes. Around six months ago, he decided to change his personal coach and began working with Croatian shooter Giovanni Cernogoraz, an Olympic gold medallist."The changes were made collectively by my personal coach and national coach. Peter Wilson helped me change my stance, while my stock was also changed. There were a few things related to my movement towards the target that we worked on. Making these changes in such a short time before the World Championships was challenging, but when you make the right changes, things start going up," he said.The 24-year-old also credited the changing atmosphere within the Indian shooting camp for the country's growing success on the international stage. He believes Wilson has brought a different mindset to the team, encouraging shooters to embrace pressure rather than be overwhelmed by it."I think 65 per cent of this sport is mental, and the biggest change has been the mental approach brought in by Peter Wilson. The enthusiasm he brings is unbelievable. We did not have anybody with us who had such great ambitions for the country. He teaches us to shout 'India' loudly in the hotel. Earlier, we were shy about these things," Kapoor said.He added that the emphasis was now on believing that Indian shooters could dominate at the highest level."You can crumble under pressure or embrace it as a privilege. You can tell yourself that this is why you are here and why you do this sport for a living. That change in mood and mentality has been a big thing for us."Kapoor's own journey into shooting began through his father, who would occasionally visit shooting ranges with his friends. Although there were no shooters in his family, the stories he heard at home sparked an early fascination with firearms.Professionally, he drew inspiration from several coaches and accomplished shooters. He particularly remembers former coach Mansher Singh for instilling discipline during his formative years and Khalid Al-Mudaf for helping him develop the mental side of the sport. He also spoke warmly about Kainan, whom he considers an important influence in his development.However, it is his current coach Cernogoraz's work ethic that has left a lasting impression."He is somebody I look up to in terms of working hard. I realised that you cannot be a champion without working like a champion. I am fortunate to see how he works, from morning to evening at the range, and then comes back and runs 10 kilometres. When you see someone like that, it motivates you," Kapoor said.With the Los Angeles Olympics now on the horizon, Kapoor is keen to keep his feet on the ground. While his performance in Doha secured an Olympic quota place for India, it does not automatically guarantee him a place in the final team. The country's selection process will involve domestic trials, making the coming competitions equally important."By God's grace, I have the points and I am going to follow a plan that I had already made," he said.He is now looking forward to domestic competitions before assessing his international schedule and possible World Cup appearances.For a shooter who has learnt to put a missed target behind him and focus on the next one, the approach towards Los Angeles remains much the same. There is no room to dwell on what could have been in Doha or get carried away by what lies ahead. As Kapoor puts it, his job is to pick up his gun every day, give his best and enjoy the sport.And perhaps that is the mindset that will define the next chapter of his journey — one target at a time, with Los Angeles firmly in sight.
Article Summary: Vivaan Kapoor won a silver medal at the World Championships in Doha. The 24-year-old believes the mental side of the sport is what separates the best from the rest. He credits the changing atmosphere within the Indian shooting camp for the country's growing success.

India produced a stirring comeback to defeat New Zealand 3-2 in the second lawn bowls test in Auckland on Tuesday, drawing level in the three-match series after losing the opening contest a day earlier.India began the second test on a positive note as the experienced Jharkhand combination of Dinesh Kumar and Sunil Bahadur registered a 6-4 victory in the men’s pairs. Article Title: Northeast has huge potential, but it’s still largely untapped: PGTI CEO Amandeep Johl
Article Text:
Amandeep Johl and Kapil Dev

Excerpts:

What is the importance of a tournament like the Masters?

How has the golf landscape in the country changed since your days as a player, coach and now CEO of PGTI?

What do you feel about the prospects of golf in the Northeast?

What do you say to people who believe golf is an elite or rich man’s sport?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

How important is golf’s return to the Olympics?

DIGBOI: Living just 250 yards from the first tee of a golf course, Amandeep Johl took up the sport at the age of seven. Since then, golf has remained an integral part of his life. In 2004, he co-founded the Asian Tour and contributed to the early institutional framework of professional golf in the region. Now serving as CEO of the Professional Golf Tour of India (PGTI), Johl spoke to TOI on the sidelines of the 26th Masters Golf Tournament here.It has grown from a small tournament and has now become a Rs 1 crore prize money event. So, it’s a very important tournament, firstly because of the prize money and secondly because it’s one of the few such tournaments in Assam and the Northeast.We are trying to promote Assam as a golf destination in India. I think Indian Oil has been a great supporter of sports, and golf in particular, as a public sector company. There is also the Petroleum Sports Control Board Golf Tournament, which has been held for many years. A lot of golfers owe their success to Indian Oil. We have golfers who have played for and secured jobs with Indian Oil.So, this tournament holds a very strategic position in the growth of golf in India because Indian Oil supports players and provides them with a livelihood through jobs and scholarships.It also organises tournaments where, once a player turns professional, they can earn prize money.I think there has been a sea change since we got Kapil Dev as the president of PGTI. Since he is a legendary cricketer who is now supporting golf, it has made a huge difference. It sends out a strong message when legends from one sport cross over to support others. He sees huge potential in this game because it is not a team sport but an individual one. There is no team selection. There is nothing that can stop someone if he or she is playing well.I feel golf in India has grown by leaps and bounds over the last two or three years. We have seen almost a 50% growth in both the number of tournaments and their prize money. With DP World joining as title sponsor, several brands such as HCL, Amul, Axis Bank, Amrutanjan, Air India, Indian Oil and Trident have also become associated with the sport. So, we feel the sky's the limit for Indian golf.The Northeast has huge potential, but it remains largely untapped, in my opinion. For example, a state like Assam can probably have four or five international-level golf courses. But there isn’t even one of that standard at the moment. We are trying to reach out to the state government because sport is a state subject. We are trying to reach out to Himanta Biswa Sarma to find out if the government can provide us with land.Golf courses can be investment magnets as well as tourism magnets. I believe India needs 300 golf courses. Even if we start building 10 every year over the next decade, we will still barely reach our potential.I don’t think it is. But even if it is, five-star hotels are also for the rich. Does the state not support them? Does an airline not have a business class? So why are we so against golf, even if it is considered an elite sport? We are trying to work towards Viksit Bharat, which aims to make India a developed nation with a per capita income of over $25,000. If that is what we are working towards, why should we be against golf? I’m not disputing that it is an elite sport, but it is also an aspirational sport.It’s very important. I think Indian girls are doing much better than the boys. We have seen players like Pranavi and Diksha Dagar perform consistently at the international level. Diksha, one of my students, has won two gold medals at the Deaflympics. She also plays regularly on the Ladies European Tour and was part of the Indian team that won silver at the Asian Games. So, I feel the girls are doing very well. But it is only a matter of time before the boys start performing too.(The writer is in Digboi on an invitation from DP World PGTI)
Article Summary: Amandeep Johl is CEO of the Professional Golf Tour of India (PGTI) He spoke to TOI on the sidelines of the 26th Masters Golf Tournament here. Johl: Golf in India has grown by leaps and bounds over the last two or three years.

NEW DELHI: Being the son of a legendary cricketer comes with its own set of expectations, and Hassan Eisakhil is beginning to understand the weight of that legacy. The 20-year-old is the son of Mohammad Nabi , one of the pioneers of Afghanistan cricket, who, at 41, continues to defy age and remains an integral part of the senior national team. Nabi has also expressed his desire to share the dressing room with his son in Afghan colours one day.Eisakhil, however, is unfazed by the expectations that come with being Mohammad Nabi's son. For now, the young opener is focused on developing his game and making a name for himself."So far, I haven't felt any pressure about being Mohammad Nabi's son. I just play my natural game. Whatever I have learnt from playing cricket, I try to put into practice. I don't do anything extra," Eisakhil told TimesofIndia.com in an interview facilitated by Sony Sports Network ahead of the Asia Cup Rising Stars, which begins on Thursday in Doha, Qatar."We talk about cricket a lot at home. I ask him questions, and he shares his experiences with me. He also points out my mistakes and watches our matches. He helps me a lot," he said.Eisakhil breaks into a smile when asked whether his father is a hard taskmaster."He is very strict during training and practice. After that, we are like friends and talk normally. So, I would say he is strict during training," he said.The father-son duo recently played together in the Bangladesh Premier League (BPL), and Eisakhil hopes that one day fans will see them represent Afghanistan together in the national jersey. It is a "dream" that Nabi expressed in 2025. The son echoes that now."Inshallah, we will play together in the national jersey as well. It depends on how I perform. If I perform really well, I will make it to the national team," Eisakhil said.Afghanistan open their campaign against Sri Lanka A on Thursday, and the young opener, who has already represented his country at the Under-19 level, is eager to make the most of the opportunity."The preparation is going well. Recently, we haven't played many ODIs, as we have been involved in a lot of T20 tournaments. So, we had a camp in Jalalabad, where we held a few practice sessions and played some intra-squad ODI matches. The preparation has been good," Eisakhil said.Eisakhil shares some batting similarities with his father, but unlike Nabi, he is a top-order batter. Having already played a couple of T20Is for Afghanistan at the Asian Games, he is aware that breaking into the senior team's established opening combination of Rahmanullah Gurbaz and Ibrahim Zadran will not be easy."The competition is very strong, but I take it as motivation to work harder. Inshallah, I will make it to the national team through my performances soon," he said.Despite being the son of one of Afghanistan's cricketing greats, Eisakhil looks up to two Indian batting stars: Virat Kohli and Shubman Gill "I would say Shubman Gill and Virat Kohli. I admire the way they maintain discipline and consistency in their work," he said."Ever since I started playing cricket in 2020, I have watched Virat Kohli play. I admire his passion for the game, his fitness levels, the way he bats and how he calculates a chase. The way he approaches and chases any target is something I really love," he added.As a top-order batter, Eisakhil is keen to incorporate some of Kohli's methods into his own game, particularly when chasing targets."I am working on that. I am trying to understand how to pace an innings and handle pressure situations. I work on these aspects with my father and Afghanistan's domestic coaches. I also ask them questions, and I am gradually getting a better understanding of the game."For now, Eisakhil is not looking too far ahead. The prospect of playing alongside his father in Afghanistan colours remains a dream, but he knows that the journey towards it will have to be built on his own performances. With Nabi's experience to draw upon and the likes of Kohli and Gill to inspire him, the 20-year-old is keen to carve out an identity of his own.
Article Summary: Hassan Eisakhil, 20, is the son of Mohammad Nabi, one of the pioneers of Afghanistan cricket. The father-son duo recently played together in the Bangladesh Premier League (BPL) The young opener is focused on developing his game and making a name for himself.

Article Title: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi needs right set of people around him: Dinesh Karthik
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (BCCI Photo)

MUMBAI: Indian cricket 's wonderkid 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is "ruling the world," but "needs a good support system, the right set of people around him, the coaches, the family," feels former India wicketkeeper Dinesh Karthik , currently IPL defending champions’ Royal Challengers Bengaluru’s batting coach and mentor."For the longest time, probably for the last half a decade maybe, that I've been part of the job. There's not an event that I've gone to where they have not asked me about Kohli or Rohit. The new one to enter the list is Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Wherever I go these days, there's a question about him. It's very interesting, isn't it? At the age of 14, I was trying to understand how to finish my maths homework and here is a kid who is ruling the world right now. But in him lies the challenge. And when I say challenge, I'm talking about society in general. And that includes people like me who hold on to a microphone and have views about him. I think it's important for a lot of precocious talent to also fall and land sometimes, understand from mistakes and have acceptance from our side. He needs what I call a really good support system, the right set of people around him, the coaches, the family.The most important people being the public who view him and people like me who are broadcasting and have a view on him," Karthik said at an Sustainable Markets Initiative event, organised by the prestigious Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) and the Mumbai Cricket Association, at the MCA Lounge in the Wankhede Stadium on Tuesday.Comparing Sooryavanshi to a young Sachin Tendulkar , Karthik said, "To understand that he's 14-years-old, understand the nature of the beast which is this game which is right now at its strongest financially in terms of the amount of people who are following this game and the different formats and the challenges that go along with it. He's a kid. And he's extraordinarily talented. You don't get that kind of talent. I think the last person who's probably as spoken about and viewed as in terms of talent is from this city, Sachin Tendulkar. So, he became the greatest ever to have played this game. As you know, we literally refer to him as the god of cricket. That's how much we regularly look up to him and what he's achieved is something that we all look up to as standard and at times unachievable. I do feel Sooryavanshi is that kind of a talent. And for him, I'd say, have a smile. Enjoy the journey."Karthik urged the fans and critics to "allow him to grow as a cricketer." "And for the rest of us, I'd say, watch what you say about him. Allow him to grow and learn as a cricketer. Because the pressures of today are very different to what it was two decades ago. I genuinely wish him the best of luck. He's an extraordinary talent. And you can't stop such a talent at the age of 14. He's that good that he's forcing his way into playing in the T20 format, which is probably one of the toughest to get into. But that's how talented he is. You don't want to stop a talent like that. But you want to make sure that the support staff around him is very strong.Unlike an emerging Tendulkar from three decades ago, Sooryavanshi has the endure the added pressure of a relentless social media. Reiterating his point about the importance of having the right kind of advisors around Sooryanbshi who would help him make the right choices in life, Karthik said, "That's the world we live in today. I know there's plenty of offers for him on the table to do various things off the field. And that's where he needs a good set of heads helping him and choosing the right position. And for the modern-day cricketer, I think there are a lot of good things about social media. But there are also a lot of things. If you don't have discipline, and you don't have the right set of eyes, you could get into the wrong sort of lane, if I could say that. So, as much as you would want to explore and become the best cricketer, you need to know where you want to draw the line. And your relationship with social media, and in general the media, is very important."Karthik advised Sooryavanshi and other young cricketers to "filter out what's important and leave out the rest." "There is no doubt that today's cricketers are under a lot more scrutiny. Because every person, even before, had a view, but they had no place to express it. But today, because of social media, every person can put their view outside. If you start looking at every opinion about you, I feel like it becomes a very hard place to live.You need to be able to kind of filter out what's important and leave out the rest," Karthik said.Meanwhile, Karthik revealed that RCB felt the pressure of defending the IPL title in 2026 much more than winning it for the first time in 2025. “The pressure of trying to defend something, hold on to something is completely alien to RCB at that stage, and to defend a title was a lot more challenging. The expectations and knowing that a group of people, or players, were hunting together, looking at the first mistake that we could make, to bounce on it and still trying to hold on to it and end up crossing the line, was definitely harder,” the 41-year-old said.
Article Summary: Former India wicketkeeper Dinesh Karthik is currently IPL defending champions’ Royal Challengers Bengaluru’s batting coach and mentor. He says Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is "ruling the world," but "needs a good support system, the right set of people around him, the coaches, the family" He urges fans and critics to "allow him to grow as a cricketer"

The All India Football Federation (AIFF) has filed a complaint with the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) over an alleged racist gesture by a Palestine player towards India U17 men's team captain Dallalmuon Gangte during their AFC U17 Asian Cup Qualifier match in Kuala Lumpur.India defeated Palestine 4-1 on Tuesday to remain unbeaten in Group E of the qualifiers for the 2027 Asian Cup. Match referee Ko Minkuk intervened to separate the two players and warned both of them.The match also saw another disciplinary incident. Palestine midfielder Mohammed Jamhour was shown a straight red card in the first half for kicking Indian player Raj Singh Wahengbam twice.In its complaint, the AIFF has asked the continental governing body to look into the incident and take necessary action.The federation has asked the AFC to "review the incident, examine the available match footage, and take appropriate action under the applicable regulations," it said in a statement posted on X.The AIFF also made its stand clear on discrimination in football.The federation said it "considers any form of racism and discriminatory behaviour extremely serious"."Such conduct is contrary to fundamental values of football, which are built on respect, equality, fair play and sportsmanship. Article Title: 'Made me feel betrayed': Cameron Bancroft blasts Australia captain Pat Cummins over 2018 ball-tampering scandal
Article Text:
Pat Cummins and Cameron Bancroft

Bancroft says the entire team knew

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cummins's denial questioned

NEW DELHI: Cameron Bancroft has reignited the 2018 Australian ball-tampering scandal by backing Usman Khawaja ’s claim that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper against South Africa.He also accused current Australia captain Pat Cummins of betrayal, saying his recent denial of knowing about the incident did not match what Bancroft experienced during the tour.Bancroft, who was banned for nine months after being caught using sandpaper on the ball, admitted that he had not revealed the full truth during Cricket Australia’s initial investigation because he wanted to protect his teammates.In an article for the West Australian, Bancroft said he decided to speak out after Cummins’ 70-minute press conference, where the captain dismissed Khawaja’s claims as “100 per cent wrong” and “irresponsible”.Explaining why he had remained silent for so long, Bancroft said, “The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference. It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.”Bancroft directly challenged the earlier version of events, under which only he, Steve Smith and David Warner were held responsible for the scandal. He insisted that other players were also aware of what was happening, including the team's fast bowlers.“It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa,” Bancroft wrote. “It was the whole team.”He further claimed that he regularly discussed the condition of the ball with Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh, as well as wicketkeeper Tim Paine.According to Bancroft, these conversations were about whether the ball was reversing enough and whether more work was needed to make it swing. He also said members of the playing and coaching staff encouraged his efforts, particularly bowling coach David Saker.Bancroft said the support he received made him believe that using sandpaper was accepted as part of the team's collective effort. He also maintained that what he witnessed during the South Africa tour was different from the public version Cummins has presented over the years.His comments come after Cricket Australia announced an independent forum where players can privately share their memories of the scandal without fear of retrospective punishment.Chief executive Todd Greenberg clarified that the move was not a formal reinvestigation, adding that both Cummins and Khawaja were entitled to their own versions of events.
Article Summary: Cameron Bancroft has reignited the 2018 Australian ball-tampering scandal. He has backed Usman Khawaja’s claim that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper against South Africa. He also accused current Australia captain Pat Cummins of betrayal, saying his recent denial of knowing about the incident did not match what he experienced.

India pacer Arshdeep Singh has emerged as one of the biggest gainers in the latest ICC Men's Player Rankings, climbing 12 places to reach a career-best joint 19th position among ODI bowlers following the conclusion of the three-match series against New Zealand. The latest update also saw England's Tom Banton make a significant jump in the batting rankings after his match-winning century against Australia, while several Zimbabwe and Afghanistan players made notable gains in the Test charts.Arshdeep climbed 12 places to share 19th position among ODI bowlers, with Afghanistan spinner Rashid Khan continuing to occupy the top spot. New Zealand pacer Matt Henry also enjoyed a major rise, moving up 15 places to joint 12th, while his teammate Kyle Jamieson gained 15 spots to reach 45th.England's Jofra Archer returned to the top 10, climbing four places to seventh after picking up a wicket in each of the first two ODIs against Australia.England batter Tom Banton was among the biggest beneficiaries in the ODI batting rankings after his match-winning century against Australia in the second ODI in Adelaide. Banton smashed 121 off 99 deliveries, registering his second ODI century to help England level the series.His performance propelled him 34 places to a career-high 13th position.His teammate Joe Root also returned to the top 10, gaining two places to reach ninth after scoring a half-century in the same match. India's Shubman Gill continues to lead the ODI batting rankings.The latest Test rankings update also reflected the performances from the closely fought series between Zimbabwe and Afghanistan in Sharjah, which Zimbabwe won 2-0. Former Australia head coach Darren Lehmann has welcomed Cricket Australia's (CA) decision to establish an independent forum to hear accounts from those involved in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, insisting he has nothing to hide and would be willing to speak.Lehmann, who was at the helm during Australia's controversial tour of South Africa in 2018 and subsequently resigned following the Cape Town scandal, believes the initiative will give people who did not get an opportunity to speak earlier a chance to share their experiences.Speaking during the third ODI between Australia and England in Hobart, Lehmann told ABC Sport: "Yeah (I would speak to them). I have got nothing to hide.""I think this gives everyone who didn't get a chance to speak [a chance now]. It gives everyone a bit of clarity for the Cricket Australia board to make a decision from there [once people are heard]. I think it is a good thing," he added. CA announced the forum on Wednesday following fresh revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr . The former Australia opener claimed that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper during the 2018 Cape Town Test and alleged that the ball had also been tampered with in the preceding Test at Gqeberha.Interim chairman David Boon said the forum would allow players and staff involved in the South Africa tour to share their experiences in a safe and respectful environment."After careful discussion, we agreed to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and their perspectives," Boon said. "We believe it is time for a circuit breaker."CA chief executive Todd Greenberg clarified that the initiative would not reopen the original investigation or lead to fresh sanctions. The board will decide what information can be made public after the process."We will look to be as transparent as we possibly can, whilst at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the people who come forward," Greenberg said."The public want to know what happened there. It's hard to get the whole truth unless everyone is speaking, support staff and players," Khawaja said on Kayo.He also questioned the board's authority to decide what information would be released, asking: "What is the outcome from this?" David Warner has echoed Khawaja's concerns, insisting the issue is about transparency and accountability rather than penalties."No, not at all, not at all. Look, we put our hands up, we accepted what Cricket Australia handed out to us... It is not about penalties. It is just about coming up with transparency and accountability," Warner said.The forum comes amid renewed disagreement over who knew about the ball-tampering plan, with current Australia captain Pat Cummins rejecting Khawaja's claims and maintaining that he had no knowledge of sandpaper being taken onto the field.

Article Title: Afghanistan's 20-year-old Naseer Khan Maroofkhil achieves rare Test double last seen in 1965
Article Text:

Nasser Khan Maroofkhil 's performance on Test debut

Innings Batting Bowling First innings 20 (74 balls) 7/151 (44 overs) Second innings 101* (242 balls) 2/106 (37 overs) Total 121 runs 9 wickets

Afghanistan's 20-year-old all-rounder Naseer Khan Maroofkhil produced a remarkable performance on his Test debut against Zimbabwe in Sharjah, entering the record books with a rare double.In the 149-year history of Test cricket, Maroofkhil became only the second player to score a century and take a five-wicket haul in the same match on debut. He also became the youngest player to achieve this feat, at the age of 20 years and 287 days.His performance was special with both bat and ball. Maroofkhil scored 20 runs off 74 balls in the first innings before making an unbeaten 101 off 242 balls in the second.With the ball, he picked up seven wickets for 151 runs in 44 overs in the first innings. He followed it up with two wickets for 106 runs in 37 overs in the second innings.Maroofkhil also created another record through his workload in the match. e faced a total of 316 balls across his two innings and bowled 81 overs, delivering 486 balls. He became the first player in Test history to face more than 300 deliveries and bowl more than 300 deliveries on his debut.He also became the first player to bat for more than 50 overs and bowl more than 50 overs in a Test debut.Before Maroofkhil, only New Zealand's Bruce Taylor had scored a century and taken a five-wicket haul on his Test debut.Taylor achieved the feat against India at Eden Gardens in Kolkata in March 1965. Batting at No. 8, he scored 105 runs in the first innings. He then took five wickets for 86 runs in 23.5 overs in India's first innings.The match ended in a draw. Taylor scored an unbeaten zero in his second innings.Maroofkhil and Taylor remain the only two players to score a century and take five wickets in an innings on their Test debut.Maroofkhil also became one of only two players to score at least 100 runs and take eight or more wickets on Test debut. The other player was Albert Trott, who scored 110 runs and took eight wickets against England in Adelaide in 1895.Maroofkhil finished his debut match with 121 runs and nine wickets against Zimbabwe. He also became the third Afghanistan player to score a century on Test debut. Rahmanullah had scored 113 against Zimbabwe in the first Test of the series earlier this month, while Ismat Alam made 101 against Zimbabwe in Bulawayo in January 2025.Maroofkhil's unbeaten 101 is the second-highest individual score by an Afghanistan batter on Test debut, behind Rahmanullah's 113.Maroofkhil is also the fourth Afghanistan bowler to take a five-wicket haul on Test debut. His figures of seven wickets for 151 runs in the first innings are the second-best by an Afghanistan bowler on debut. Ziaur Rahman holds the record with seven wickets for 97 runs in the first innings of his maiden Test.
Article Summary: Afghanistan's 20-year-old all-rounder Naseer Khan Maroofkhil produced a remarkable performance on his Test debut against Zimbabwe. He became only the second player to score a century and take a five-wicket haul in the same match on debut. He also became the youngest player to achieve this feat, at the age of 20 years and 287 days.

Article Title: Cues from Wellington nets: Shubman Gill, Morne Morkel and '20 good balls'

"20 good balls, yeah?" was Shubman Gill 's polite request to Morne Morkel as the duo prepared for an intriguing contest. The practice pitch with the thickest grass cover was the centre of attention as Morkel stood at the top of his mark, some three yards inside the crease. With a mitt in hand, Morkel began firing throwdowns at Gill, who wasn't amused by the ball being hidden inside the oversized glove."Why is the ball in the mitt? Bowlers don't have a mitt," Gill remarked, prompting Morkel to chuckle. "Aah, for the reverse swing," the bowling coach replied.The Indian captain tapped the spot around a good length and asked Morkel to bowl there with a semi-old ball and a scrambled seam. The bowling coach put the right-hander's defence to the test, finding his edge on two occasions and even beating him through the gate with a delivery that came in with the angle. A mini-celebration followed as the lanky fast bowler looked skywards before asking if the moment had been recorded.Gill, meanwhile, got back to business and adopted a tighter approach against the deliveries that followed.He tweaked his trigger movement ever so slightly and looked much more assured after the early wobble. Throwdown specialist Dayanand Garani continued to angle deliveries into the right-hander's pads, but Gill wasn't pleased with those lines.He asked Garani to bowl in a better channel and target the areas where he could challenge his defence. He even explained why the existing line wasn't troubling him enough.The exercise continued for close to 30 minutes before Gill called out, "Final two", wrapping up what was a productive batting workout ahead of the series opener at the Basin Reserve in Wellington. A thick covering of grass, notorious winds and challenging conditions await Gill and Co.from November 19. India have plenty of batting experience in their ranks, but come Thursday, the challenge will be to translate the lessons from the nets into performance against a potent bowling attack.India endured a forgettable batting series the last time they toured these shores. If they are to return with a favourable result this time, much will depend on how their batters adapt to the conditions. The visitors have enough talent and X-factor in their ranks, but the series will be finely poised only if they can put enough runs on the board for their bowlers to work with.India's batting came good during their last away tour of England in 2025, and Gill will hope to replicate his prolific run from that memorable summer. For now, the focus is on getting through those 20 good balls, one delivery at a time.
